Equivalence and Noninferiority Tests for Two Paired Proportions

Source: R/equivalence_proportion_paired.R
equivalence_proportion_paired.Rd

Tests whether the difference between two proportions measured on the same units, \(\psi = p_x - p_y\), lies inside equivalence bounds or above a noninferiority margin: whether a cheaper diagnostic procedure finds a condition about as often as the standard one on the same patients, or whether a short form of a scale classifies respondents about as often as the full form. The tests are the score tests of Nam (1997), which take the place of the t tests of equivalence_c, and the decisions are read from the score interval of ci_proportion_paired (Tango, 1998), with which they agree.

Usage

equivalence_proportion_paired(
  x = NULL,
  y = NULL,
  n_10 = NULL,
  n_01 = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  prop_diff_lower = NULL,
  prop_diff_upper = NULL,
  alpha_level = 0.05
)

Arguments

x, y

Numeric or logical vectors of the same length, one element per unit, coded 1 (success) and 0 (failure): the outcome of each unit under the first condition (x) and the second (y). A pair with a missing value in either vector is dropped. Supply either x and y or the three counts, not both.

n_10

Number of units that succeed under x and fail under y.

n_01

Number of units that fail under x and succeed under y.

N

Number of units (pairs), at least n_10 + n_01.

prop_diff_lower, prop_diff_upper

Bounds on the scale of the difference in proportions, each a single number in (0, 1); the equivalence region is \((-\delta_L, \delta_U)\), with prop_diff_lower as \(\delta_L\) and prop_diff_upper as \(\delta_U\). Supply at least one. With prop_diff_upper alone the bounds are symmetric. With prop_diff_lower alone the call is a noninferiority test with margin \(\delta_L\), and the rows that would need an upper bound are NA (see Details).

alpha_level

One-sided significance level of each test. Defaults to 0.05, so the decisions are read from the 90% score interval.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with rows difference (\(\hat\psi\)); the counts n_10, n_01, and N; the score statistics z_lower (\(Z(-\delta_L)\)) and z_upper (\(Z(\delta_U)\)) and their one-sided p-values p_lower and p_upper; the TOST p-value p_tost; the noninferiority p-value p_noninferiority (equal to p_lower by construction); the 100(1 - 2\(\alpha\))% score limits ci_lower and ci_upper; the bounds prop_diff_lower (stored signed, as \(-\delta_L\)) and prop_diff_upper; and the flags equivalent, noninferior, superior, inferior, and nonsuperior (1 = declared, 0 = not). A noninferiority test alone, with no prop_diff_upper, has the same rows, with NA in those that would need an upper bound. The attributes are conf_level (\(1 - 2\alpha\)), the verdict, and p_sentence, which names the p-value results_sentence reports beside the interval: p_tost, or p_noninferiority for a noninferiority test alone.

Details

The tests. With the score statistic \(Z(\psi_0)\) described on ci_proportion_paired, the noninferiority null hypothesis \(H_0: \psi \le -\delta_L\) is rejected in favor of \(\psi > -\delta_L\) when \(Z(-\delta_L) > z_{1-\alpha}\), and the nonsuperiority null hypothesis \(H_0: \psi \ge \delta_U\) is rejected in favor of \(\psi < \delta_U\) when \(Z(\delta_U) < -z_{1-\alpha}\). Equivalence, \(-\delta_L < \psi < \delta_U\), is claimed when both are rejected. Because the claim requires both rejections, the two one-sided tests form an intersection-union test (Berger & Hsu, 1996): each is carried out at level \(\alpha\) and the equivalence claim has level \(\alpha\), with no adjustment for there being two tests. The p-value of the equivalence test, p_tost, is the larger of the two one-sided p-values.

Why the score statistic and not McNemar's. McNemar's test estimates the variance of the per-unit difference as it would be if \(\psi\) were 0, so it tests no difference and nothing else. A test against a margin needs the variance at \(\psi = -\delta_L\) (or \(\delta_U\)), which depends on a discordant probability that the hypothesis does not fix; the score statistic replaces that probability with its maximum likelihood estimate under the hypothesis (Nam, 1997). At \(\psi_0 = 0\) the score statistic is McNemar's, so the tests here generalize it. Nam (1997) found that a Wald-type statistic, with the variance estimated from the observed proportions instead, rejects more often than its nominal level, while the score test holds close to it.

Reading the interval. \(Z\) decreases in \(\psi_0\), and the score interval is the set of differences the score test does not reject. So the noninferiority test rejects at level \(\alpha\) exactly when the lower limit of the 100(1 - 2\(\alpha\))% score interval exceeds \(-\delta_L\), and the nonsuperiority test exactly when its upper limit is below \(\delta_U\). The flags are computed from that interval, which the table reports.

The flags and the verdict. The flags read the interval against the bounds:

  • equivalent: the interval lies inside \((-\delta_L, \delta_U)\).

  • noninferior: the lower limit exceeds \(-\delta_L\).

  • superior: the lower limit exceeds \(\delta_U\).

  • inferior: the upper limit is below \(-\delta_L\).

  • nonsuperior: the upper limit is below \(\delta_U\), so a difference in favor of x as large as \(\delta_U\) is ruled out. It is the mirror image of noninferiority.

With both bounds, the "verdict" attribute names the most informative statement the interval supports: "Equivalent", "Superior", "Inferior", "Noninferior only" (an interval above \(-\delta_L\) that contains \(\delta_U\)), "Not relevantly superior only" (an interval below \(\delta_U\) that contains \(-\delta_L\)), or "Inconclusive" (an interval that contains both bounds). An inconclusive result is a statement about precision, not evidence of a difference.

Noninferiority alone. A call with prop_diff_lower and no prop_diff_upper asks only whether \(\psi > -\delta_L\), and no upper bound is assumed for it. The rows that would need one, z_upper, p_upper, p_tost, prop_diff_upper, equivalent, superior, and nonsuperior, are NA, so the table keeps its shape; the verdict is "Noninferior" (the lower limit exceeds \(-\delta_L\)), "Inferior" (the upper limit is below \(-\delta_L\)), or "Inconclusive"; and the p-value a results sentence reports is p_noninferiority. This is the noninferiority test of equivalence_c, which reads \(-\delta_L\) alone. A call with prop_diff_upper alone gives the symmetric bounds \((-\delta_U, \delta_U)\), as equivalence_c does.

Choosing the bounds. The bounds are fixed before the data are examined, on substantive grounds, as the smallest difference in the two proportions that would matter, and on the scale of the difference itself: prop_diff_lower = 0.05 is five percentage points.

References

Berger, R. L., & Hsu, J. C. (1996). Bioequivalence trials, intersection-union tests and equivalence confidence sets. Statistical Science, 11(4), 283–319. doi:10.1214/ss/1032280304

McNeil, B. J., Keeler, E., & Adelstein, S. J. (1975). Primer on certain elements of medical decision making. New England Journal of Medicine, 293(5), 211–215. doi:10.1056/NEJM197507312930501

Nam, J.-m. (1997). Establishing equivalence of two treatments and sample size requirements in matched-pairs design. Biometrics, 53(4), 1422–1430. doi:10.2307/2533508

Tango, T. (1998). Equivalence test and confidence interval for the difference in proportions for the paired-sample design. Statistics in Medicine, 17(8), 891–908. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19980430)17:8<891::AID-SIM780>3.0.CO;2-B

ci_proportion_paired for the interval alone; equivalence_c for a linear contrast of means.

Examples

# Liver scan data from McNeil, Keeler, and Adelstein (1975), the
# example of Nam (1997, p. 1427): 344 patients classified by scan (x)
# and by pathology (y), 32 positive by scan only and 27 by pathology
# only. Does the scan understate the rate of disease by less than five
# percentage points? That is a noninferiority question, so only
# prop_diff_lower is given, and the rows that would need an upper bound
# are NA. z_lower is the score statistic Nam reports, 2.795; the table
# rounds it for display and stores the full value.
res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 32, n_01 = 27, N = 344,
                                     prop_diff_lower = 0.05)
res
#>  term             value 
#>  difference       0.015 
#>  n_10             32    
#>  n_01             27    
#>  N                344   
#>  z_lower          2.795 
#>  z_upper          <NA>  
#>  p_lower          0.0026
#>  p_upper          <NA>  
#>  p_tost           <NA>  
#>  p_noninferiority 0.0026
#>  ci_lower         -0.023
#>  ci_upper         0.052 
#>  prop_diff_lower  -0.050
#>  prop_diff_upper  <NA>  
#>  equivalent       <NA>  
#>  noninferior      1     
#>  superior         <NA>  
#>  inferior         0     
#>  nonsuperior      <NA>  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
res$value[res$term == "z_lower"]
#> [1] 2.795403
attr(res, "verdict")
#> [1] "Noninferior"

# Agreement within five points in both directions is a stronger
# claim. The interval rules out a shortfall of five points but not an
# excess of five, so the verdict is noninferiority only.
res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 32, n_01 = 27, N = 344,
                                     prop_diff_lower = 0.05,
                                     prop_diff_upper = 0.05)
attr(res, "verdict")
#> [1] "Noninferior only"

# A short form (x) and the full form (y) of a screening scale given to
# the same 400 respondents: 38 screen positive on the short form only
# and 52 on the full form only. A shortfall of five points is not ruled
# out, but an excess of five is.
res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 38, n_01 = 52, N = 400,
                                     prop_diff_lower = 0.05,
                                     prop_diff_upper = 0.05)
res
#>  term             value 
#>  difference       -0.035
#>  n_10             38    
#>  n_01             52    
#>  N                400   
#>  z_lower          0.632 
#>  z_upper          -3.498
#>  p_lower          0.2636
#>  p_upper          0.0002
#>  p_tost           0.2636
#>  p_noninferiority 0.2636
#>  ci_lower         -0.074
#>  ci_upper         0.004 
#>  prop_diff_lower  -0.050
#>  prop_diff_upper  0.050 
#>  equivalent       0     
#>  noninferior      0     
#>  superior         0     
#>  inferior         0     
#>  nonsuperior      1     
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
attr(res, "verdict")
#> [1] "Not relevantly superior only"
